title: Differentiation II: Beyond-Product (Alternative) Differentiation
keyQuestion: Is beyond-product differentiation better or worse than product differentiation?

reading.name: Differentiation Brief (re-read) — no new brief for this session

case.name: A More Company: Valuation or Value Creation

slides: No slides for this session (Canvas). The last S9 slide shows the Clegg Auto / A More Company logo.

framework.name: Beyond-product differentiation, judged with the Differentiation Brief
framework.summary: Product differentiation raises WTP through the offering itself (performance, features). Beyond-product differentiation raises WTP — or lowers cost — through what surrounds the product: the people who deliver it, the trust they earn, the ownership and governance that make promises credible, the community and movement around the firm. Judge it with the same tests: does the buyer perceive and pay, which source of WTP is it, which durability mechanism protects it, and where does the gain land?

components.name: People as the differentiation engine
components.what: Porter's third engine: 'people, where the encounter is the product' (Ritz-Carlton, Chick-fil-A, USAA, Nordstrom). Clegg's theory: a business that helps a person progress toward what they want produces an employee who cares, who produces work customers value.

components.name: Trust in a market the buyer cannot verify
components.what: Auto repair is a trust/credence business: 'customers cannot verify the work and must believe the person recommending it.' The brief's own example: 63% of US drivers don't trust repair shops, 64% say they've found one they do.

components.name: Credible commitment through structure
components.what: A perpetual purpose employee ownership trust: the company can never be sold; liquidation goes to charity; five purposes are legally permanent. 'A firm that can walk back a commitment has not made one' — the trust converts a promise into a structure rivals (PE roll-ups) won't sign.

components.name: Social complexity and causal ambiguity
components.what: An operating culture of 'genuine care' lived in thousands of small moments is socially complex and hard to specify — hard to copy, but also hard to build and verify.

components.name: Where the gain lands
components.what: Engaged, experienced technicians → fewer comebacks, more honest tickets, reputation that fills bays without advertising. Some of that lands in price/volume (WTP); some lands in cost (lower turnover, rework, marketing) — and 'a gain that shows up entirely in cost is an operating improvement, not differentiation.'

components.name: Three networks
components.what: Movement (idea; weakest economic case; low cost to run), community (shared place; moderate), vertical (operational overlap; strongest, direct and measurable; high cost). Failure modes: enthusiasm without practice; stays a chamber of commerce; members join for savings and skip the idea.

terms.def: A trust that holds the operating businesses permanently for the benefit of employees; can never be sold; ten percent of profits to charity; liquidation proceeds go to charity.

Employee stock ownership plan: a retirement trust holding company stock; employees accumulate shares and the company must repurchase them at appraised value when they leave (6,411 US ESOP companies, 15.1M participants, 2023). Clegg's objection: it points everyone at valuation, not value creation, and repurchase obligations and outside offers can force a sale.
Begin with the person's life, then career, then the company; 'the structure is downstream; it protects the idea.'

Clegg's operating shift: help each person turn a large goal into a step measured in days or weeks; replaced the formal monthly one-on-one with frequent, informal contact plus a monthly manager mastermind.
Keep It Evergreen; Own This Together; Dare To Care; Pay It Forward (≥10% of distributable profits); Expand The Circle.
Private equity roll-up: valuation. Trust model: value creation.

claims.claim: Clegg's theory of value is a claim about causation, not morale: investing in what the person is trying to build → an employee who cares → products and service customers value.
When an investor owns the butcher shop, the butcher holds no residual claim on the value created; gains flow to financial owners while risks (layoffs) stay with workers.
A coaching program depends on managers, and managers leave; the goal is an operating culture where self-management and genuine care are simply how the place runs.

Exhibit 3 tradeoffs: the trust model's source of operating advantage is engagement (tenure, trust, service quality, reputation) vs. PE's scale, consolidation, pricing power and cost reduction; its failure modes are slow growth, founder dependence and capital starvation (it cannot sell equity).
Differentiation only counts if the buyer perceives it and pays (or is willing to pay) for it.

In credence markets differentiation cannot be demonstrated, only signaled, and the signals carry real economic weight; reputation pays — a one-star rating increase raised revenue 5-9%, entirely among independents (zero for chains).

failures.name: Perceived but not paid
failures.what: Employee care that customers never experience as a reason to pay more or come back is a cost, not differentiation.

failures.name: Gain lands only in cost
failures.what: If engagement shows up only as lower turnover/rework, it is an operating improvement (still valuable, but a different advantage).

failures.name: Uneven practice
failures.what: About a quarter of the workforce consistently in the conversations; the practice is 'real, uneven and unfinished'.

failures.name: Three internal objections
failures.what: Managers lack the skill; employees believe the company has no business in their personal life; production demands crowd out the work.

failures.name: Capital starvation / founder dependence
failures.what: The trust cannot raise equity; growth from cash flow and debt only; Clegg 'has never been busier'.

caseFacts.fact: 2022: four operating businesses moved into a perpetual purpose employee ownership trust; owners (Kevin included) were paid in a negotiated sale to the trust — 'the owner still gets an exit'.
caseFacts.why: The structure is a credible commitment that employees and mission will never be subordinated to a future owner.

caseFacts.fact: First full fiscal year (2023): employee profit distributions rose from ~$40,000 to ~$400,000, without raising prices.
caseFacts.why: Ambiguous evidence: profit grew without price moving — per the brief's diagnostic, that gain landed in cost/volume, not a price premium.

caseFacts.fact: Summer 2026: best revenue month in company history; about a quarter of the workforce consistently making progress on what matters most.
caseFacts.why: Early, correlational evidence; the case cautions the 25% figure is easy to misread.

caseFacts.fact: Gallup H1 2026: 31% of US employees engaged, 51% not engaged, 18% actively disengaged (global: 20/64/16).
caseFacts.why: The 'zombie worker' problem the idea targets — and the size of the gap a genuinely engaged workforce could exploit.

caseFacts.fact: Holub (regenerative farming) and Felser (Class B camper vans) changed their companies after a conversation about the idea, not the structure.
caseFacts.why: Suggests the idea travels across industries (movement network) — but conversion takes many conversations.

caseFacts.fact: Clegg's three goals: deepen the practice in the shops (prove it works with blue-collar employees at full coverage), launch the movement, build the networks (movement, community, vertical).
caseFacts.why: The decision on the table: sequence and focus of scarce founder attention.

caseFacts.fact: 51% of owners of employer businesses are 55 or older; small businesses that outlive founders are increasingly sold to PE roll-ups (buy low, cut costs, consolidate, raise prices, exit).
caseFacts.why: The supply of founders facing the exit decision — the market for the model.

strongAnalysis: Define terms: product differentiation = the offering itself is better on a dimension buyers value; beyond-product = WTP from the people, trust, ownership and community around the offering (Porter's 'people' engine; the brief's 'trust' and 'identity' sources).

Better (durability): beyond-product differentiation tends to rest on social complexity, causal ambiguity, path dependence and credible commitment — the four mechanisms that make a premium last — whereas product features are routinely copied (Casper) or normalized (Peloton). A perpetual trust is a commitment a PE-owned rival will not sign.
Better (fit to the market): in a credence business like auto repair, the product can't be verified, so trust IS the product; honest tickets and fewer comebacks are exactly what the buyer pays for.

Worse (measurability and verification): the payoff lives in customers' heads and is slow; the case's evidence is mostly cost/volume ($40k → $400k distributions without price increases; best revenue month), not a demonstrated price premium. It's hard to scale (one conversation at a time; 25% coverage), founder-dependent, and capital-constrained.

Judgment: beyond-product differentiation is more durable but harder to build and prove; it is 'better' where the product is a credence good and the encounter is the product, and only if the firm can show the premium or retention in the accounts. Clegg's sequencing logic: deepen the practice first — a claim that it works anywhere is worth little until it works everywhere in one place.

counter.argument: Beyond-product differentiation is just good management (operational effectiveness): engaged employees lower turnover and rework — that's a cost improvement any well-run shop can copy, not a strategy.
counter.response: Partly right — the brief says a gain that lands only in cost is an operating improvement. But the case's mechanism is trust in a credence market (honest tickets, reputation that fills bays), which lands in WTP and volume. What rivals can't copy is not 'be nice to employees' but the bundle: a structure that can't be sold, a culture lived across thousands of small moments, and years of accumulated reputation (path dependence + social complexity + credible commitment). The burden is on Clegg to show it in retention, comebacks and price realization.

courseMap.text: Extends S9's differentiation from product to people, trust and governance; connects to VRIO's imitability barriers (S6) and to S11's question of whether a firm can win on both cost and WTP (engagement can do both).
